title: Hayward
name: Hayward
metaTitle: 1031 Exchange Hayward CA | 1031 Exchange San Francisco
metaDescription: Hayward 1031 exchange coordination for industrial, distribution, and warehouse owners along the I-880 corridor, including seismic diligence near the fault.

sections.html: Hayward runs on the I-880 corridor and a distribution tenant base that mostly doesn't sleep, which changes how a facilities team thinks about any maintenance or capital work here. It also sits directly over the Hayward Fault, so seismic diligence isn't a box to check once and forget, it's a recurring conversation with every serious buyer. I've never closed a Hayward deal where the buyer's facilities lead didn't ask about the fault line before asking about the rent roll, and that order of priorities tells you something about this market.

sections.heading: An Industrial City With a Distribution Backbone
sections.html:
Hayward's commercial base is dominated by industrial and logistics product, with a few other categories mixed in:

  • Distribution and warehouse buildings along the I-880 and I-580 interchange
  • Light-manufacturing and flex space serving smaller producers
  • Older retail strip centers along Foothill and Hesperian Boulevards
  • Office and light-commercial space near the Cal State East Bay area
  • Aviation-adjacent industrial parcels near Hayward Executive Airport

The interchange access that makes this corridor attractive to distribution tenants also means clear-height and dock-door count matter more to leasing than almost anything else about the building, ahead of finish quality or even location within the corridor.

sections.heading: Identifying Replacements in an Industrial-Heavy Market
sections.html: A seller exiting a distribution or warehouse asset here can often stay with the three-property rule if comparable industrial product is available nearby, since Hayward's logistics market is deep enough to support that. A seller trading an older retail strip center sometimes needs the 200% rule instead, since a repositioning play might mean comparing retail against light-industrial or flex alternatives. Whichever rule applies, I ask the qualified intermediary to confirm each candidate's seismic retrofit status before it's finalized, since that detail can change a lender's appetite for the deal later.

sections.heading: The Downtime a 24-Hour Tenant Won't Give You
sections.html: A distribution tenant running around-the-clock operations doesn't have a convenient window for dock leveler repairs, roof work, or electrical upgrades, so any capital plan has to be planned around their operating schedule, not a standard business-hours assumption. I always ask a buyer's facilities lead to get the tenant's actual operating hours and any existing maintenance restrictions before closing, because that detail changes how quickly deferred repairs can realistically get done. A roof repair that would take a weekend on a vacant building can stretch into a multi-week project once it has to be staged around active shipping lanes, and pricing that difference in advance saves a buyer from an unpleasant surprise on the first capital request.

sections.heading: Seismic Diligence Isn't Optional Here
sections.html: Because the Hayward Fault runs directly beneath the city, seismic retrofit history and structural condition deserve the same level of scrutiny as the rent roll, especially on older industrial and retail buildings that predate current code. I keep that engineering review running alongside the qualified intermediary and lender timeline so a structural surprise doesn't surface after the 45-day identification window has already closed. A structural engineer's report on an older tilt-up warehouse is worth the cost even on a deal that otherwise looks straightforward, since tilt-up construction has its own well-documented seismic vulnerabilities.

sections.heading: What a Strong Hayward Exchange Looks Like
sections.html: The investors who do well here treat tenant operating hours and seismic condition as core diligence items from the start, rather than issues to sort out once the 180-day exchange period is already running short. Both of those items are cheap to check early and expensive to discover late.

faqs.q: Does the Hayward Fault actually affect commercial property diligence?
faqs.a: Yes. Structural and seismic retrofit history deserve real scrutiny on Hayward buildings, particularly older industrial and retail stock built before current code, since the fault runs directly beneath the city. A buyer should ask for any existing structural engineering reports rather than relying only on a general property condition assessment.

faqs.q: How do you schedule maintenance on a warehouse with a 24-hour tenant?
faqs.a: It starts with getting the tenant's actual operating schedule and any existing restrictions in writing, then building the capital plan around windows the tenant can tolerate. Assuming standard business-hours access on a round-the-clock distribution tenant is a common and costly mistake, and one that shows up quickly in a tenant relations problem if a new owner gets it wrong.

faqs.q: How many replacement properties should I identify if I'm exiting Hayward industrial?
faqs.a: Three is often sufficient, since comparable warehouse and distribution product is available along the I-880 corridor. A broader list under the 200% rule usually comes up when a seller wants to compare industrial against retail or flex alternatives instead, or when the seller is also weighing candidates outside Hayward along the same interchange.

faqs.q: Is an older Foothill Boulevard retail center a good 1031 replacement?
faqs.a: It can be, but many of these centers need real repositioning to stay competitive, so a buyer should budget for tenant mix changes and possibly structural upgrades rather than assuming the existing lease roll holds indefinitely. A comparison against nearby center vacancy rates gives a more honest read than the seller's own leasing projections.

faqs.q: Can 1031 Exchange San Francisco confirm my Hayward property qualifies as an exchange?
faqs.a: No. This service coordinates identification, scheduling, and communication among the investor's advisors. Whether a specific property and transaction qualify is a determination made by the investor's CPA, tax attorney, and qualified intermediary, particularly where seismic retrofit condition affects the property's value or financing.
